section_summary: This section traces Japanese emigration policy and settlement from 1930 through 1933, concentrating on Brazil and São Paulo while also discussing Peru, Manchuria, and other possible destinations. It includes diplomatic reports, statistical memoranda, public correspondence expressing racial and strategic anxieties, and a detailed study of the government-subsidized system that recruited, processed, transported, and settled Japanese farming families in Brazil. The records emphasize that Brazil was Japan’s principal emigration outlet but could absorb only a small fraction of Japan’s annual population increase.

subfiles.title: Comment on Ambassador Ariyoshi’s Article on Japanese Emigration
subfiles.doc_type: document file note and consular despatch
subfiles.from: C. R. Cameron, American Consul General, São Paulo
subfiles.about: Comments on an article by Ambassador Akira Ariyoshi and assesses Japanese immigration and settlement in Brazil.
subfiles.summary: Cameron corrects Ariyoshi’s unfavorable characterization of Brazilian foreign ministers and supplies statistics showing rapid growth in Japanese immigration to São Paulo during the 1920s. He describes Japanese immigrants’ agricultural occupations, economic advancement, social cohesion, and efforts to learn Portuguese and display loyalty to Brazil. He concludes that Japan appears to favor gradual, geographically dispersed settlement accompanied by cultural and diplomatic efforts to forestall exclusion.

subfiles.title: Instruction Concerning the Number of Japanese Residents in Peru
subfiles.from: Francis White, for the Secretary of State
subfiles.to: Fred Morris Dearing, American Ambassador, Lima
subfiles.about: Requests an explanation of the discrepancy between estimates of 30,000 and 18,401 Japanese residents in Peru.
subfiles.summary: The Department notes that Major Allen reported 30,000 Japanese in Peru, while official Japanese statistics for 1929 listed 18,401. Ambassador Dearing is instructed to consult the Military Attaché and report which figure appears more accurate.

subfiles.title: Treatment of Japanese Nationals in Peru after the Revolution
subfiles.from: C. J. Allen, Major, General Staff
subfiles.about: Reports Japanese diplomatic protests over looting and violence against Japanese residents in revolutionary Peru.
subfiles.summary: Saburō Kurusu tells Allen that Japanese shops and plantations have been looted and that the Peruvian authorities have not provided adequate protection. Kurusu fears that publicity in Japan could turn the issue into a political controversy and reports that some Japanese residents have even suggested naval intervention. Allen describes Kurusu as friendly to the United States and repeats his estimate that 30,000 Japanese live in Peru.

subfiles.title: Japanese Subjects Resident Abroad
subfiles.from: Arthur Garrels, American Consul General, Tokyo
subfiles.about: Transmits Japanese Foreign Office statistics on Japanese residents abroad and government-assisted emigration to Brazil.
subfiles.summary: The despatch reports that 759,439 Japanese subjects were recorded abroad on October 1, 1929, and presents annual totals for 1920–1929. It explains that the United States and Australia were no longer considered viable destinations and that Japan increasingly subsidized family emigration to Brazil. A country-by-country table records Japanese populations throughout the Americas, Asia, Europe, Africa, and Japanese-controlled territories.

subfiles.title: Embassy Reply on the Japanese Population of Peru
subfiles.from: Fred Morris Dearing, American Ambassador, Lima
subfiles.about: Evaluates conflicting estimates of the Japanese population in Peru.
subfiles.summary: Dearing reports that Peru maintains no reliable statistics on resident foreigners. The Japanese Minister, who had earlier given the figure of 30,000 during serious unrest, later told an embassy officer that there were about 18,000 Japanese. The Chinese Minister nevertheless estimated at least 30,000, suggesting that Japanese official figures might omit women and children.

subfiles.title: Acknowledgment to Lucille de Liers
subfiles.from: Walter C. Thurston, for the Secretary of State
subfiles.about: Acknowledges de Liers’s comments concerning Japanese immigration into Latin American states.
subfiles.summary: The Department acknowledges receipt of de Liers’s letter of April 30, 1931. It states only that her comments on Japanese immigration into Latin America have been noted.

subfiles.title: Lucille de Liers Inquiry about Japanese Emigration
subfiles.from: Lucille de Liers
subfiles.about: Asks whether Japanese emigration to Latin America is connected with Japan’s alleged ambition for world power.
subfiles.summary: De Liers asks whether the movement of large numbers of Japanese to Latin America has a strategic or imperial purpose. She also asks whether the United States should provide territory or some other destination for Japanese emigrants.

subfiles.title: Acknowledgment to John Desmond
subfiles.from: Walter C. Thurston, for the Secretary of State
subfiles.about: Acknowledges Desmond’s comments on Japanese immigration into Latin American states.
subfiles.summary: The Department acknowledges Desmond’s letter of April 30, 1931. It records that his comments concerning Japanese immigration into Latin America have been noted.

subfiles.title: John Desmond Letter on Asian Migration and American Foreign Policy
subfiles.from: John Desmond
subfiles.about: Expresses racial and strategic alarm about Asian migration into South America and requests Senator Borah’s views.
subfiles.summary: Desmond claims that Japanese and other Asian peoples are entering South American countries with largely nonwhite populations. His argument draws comparisons with racial conditions in the United States and invokes Washington and the Monroe Doctrine in warning about future conflict. He asks for information concerning Senator Borah and the Senate Foreign Relations Committee.

subfiles.title: Acknowledgment to Martin Deardorf
subfiles.from: Walter C. Thurston, for the Secretary of State
subfiles.about: Acknowledges Deardorf’s comments on Japanese immigration into Latin American states.
subfiles.summary: The Department acknowledges Deardorf’s letter of April 30, 1931. It notes his comments about Japanese immigration into Latin America without offering a substantive reply.

subfiles.title: Martin Deardorf Letter on Japanese Settlement in Latin America
subfiles.from: Martin Deardorf
subfiles.about: Argues that organized Japanese migration could allow Japan to dominate Latin American countries and asks what the United States should do.
subfiles.summary: Deardorf asserts that most Latin American countries are being overrun by people from the “Orient,” contrasting them with Chile, Argentina, and Uruguay. He claims that Japan is deliberately transporting selected settlers aboard specially built ships and predicts that they will eventually dominate their destination countries. He requests information on the subject and urges a United States response.

subfiles.title: Acknowledgment to Stephen J. Casper Jr.
subfiles.from: Walter C. Thurston, for the Secretary of State
subfiles.about: Acknowledges Casper’s comments about Japanese immigration into Latin American states.
subfiles.summary: The Department acknowledges Casper’s letter of April 30, 1931. It states that his comments on Japanese immigration into Latin America have been noted.

subfiles.title: Stephen J. Casper Jr. Inquiry about Alleged Japanese Colonization
subfiles.from: Stephen J. Casper Jr.
subfiles.about: Requests information about reports of a Japanese government program to send large numbers of trained settlers to South America.
subfiles.summary: Casper reports allegations that Japan has set a large annual quota of skilled emigrants for South America and gives them military training before departure. He interprets the movement as an effort toward eventual Japanese colonization of the continent. He identifies Uruguay, Argentina, and Chile among the destinations and asks the Department for further information.

subfiles.title: Japanese Settlement in the Philippines, Southeast Asia, and the South Seas
subfiles.from: American Embassy, Tokyo
subfiles.about: References a despatch concerning Japanese settlement outside the Americas, especially in the Philippines, Dutch East Indies, Malay States, and mandated islands.
subfiles.summary: The sheet points to Tokyo despatch no. 77. Its abstract notes that public discussion emphasized migration to the Americas even though substantial numbers of Japanese had gradually settled in Southeast Asia and the South Seas, particularly on islands under Japanese mandate.

subfiles.title: Japanese Emigration to Manchuria
subfiles.from: Joseph C. Grew, American Embassy, Japan
subfiles.about: Reports that large-scale Japanese settlement in Manchuria had not begun, although a project for armed ex-servicemen was under consideration.
subfiles.summary: The extract states that emigration opportunities were cited as a justification for Japanese control of Manchuria, but that insecurity made most districts unsuitable for farmers. The Ministry of Overseas Affairs considered the territory unready for settlement. A proposal existed to settle one thousand armed ex-servicemen annually, but no definitive announcement had been made.

subfiles.title: Project for Sending 10,000 Japanese Emigrants to Brazil
subfiles.doc_type: document file note, embassy despatch, and statistical enclosures
subfiles.from: Joseph C. Grew, American Ambassador to Japan
subfiles.about: Reports a Japanese budget proposal to send 10,000 emigrants to Brazil and compares Brazil with Manchuria as a settlement outlet.
subfiles.summary: Grew reports an appropriation in the supplemental budget for sending 10,000 people to Brazil as part of rural-relief policy. He argues that Brazil offers climate and economic advantages over Manchuria and extends a comparatively cordial welcome, although Japan loses greater political control over emigrants there. The despatch concludes that Brazil will remain the principal government-favored outlet unless settlement in Manchuria proves more successful. Enclosures tabulate Japanese populations in Latin America and Japanese emigration by destination.

subfiles.title: Japanese Emigration to Latin American Countries, Especially Brazil
subfiles.from: Department of State, Treaty Division
subfiles.about: Reviews the history, governmental encouragement, scale, and recent restriction of Japanese emigration to Brazil and other Latin American countries.
subfiles.summary: The memorandum expands on a 1932 Treaty Division study and identifies Brazil as Japan’s most promising large-scale emigration destination after restrictions elsewhere. It reviews settlement since 1908, Japanese government passage assistance, colonization-company activities, and competing proposals for settlement in Hokkaido, Korea, Manchuria, Formosa, Mongolia, Mexico, and Peru. Brazil’s economic crisis and decrees restricting immigration in 1931–1932 sharply reduced prospects, but Japanese planners had not abandoned colonization there. The memorandum stresses that even tens of thousands of emigrants annually could not solve Japan’s population problem.

subfiles.title: Policy and Practice Governing Japanese Labor Emigration to the United States
subfiles.from: Department of State, Treaty Division
subfiles.about: References a memorandum reviewing Japanese restrictions on labor emigration to the United States from 1896 through the 1911 treaty period.
subfiles.summary: The cross-reference identifies a Treaty Division memorandum on Japanese governmental policy toward labor emigration to the United States. Its abstract states that the memorandum covers the period from 1896 through the Treaty of Commerce and Navigation of 1911 and discusses the contemporary status of Japanese emigration.

subfiles.title: Japanese Emigration to Brazil
subfiles.doc_type: document file note and consular report
subfiles.from: Robert Mills McClintock, American Vice Consul, Kobe
subfiles.about: Provides a comprehensive study of the institutions, subsidies, transportation, emigrants, and settlements involved in Japanese migration to Brazil.
subfiles.summary: McClintock describes Brazil as Japan’s principal overseas-settlement outlet while emphasizing that annual migration was negligible compared with Japan’s natural population increase. He examines the Ministry of Overseas Affairs, Kaigai Kogyo Kaisha, Kobe Emigrants’ House, and Osaka Shosen Kaisha, explaining how the state recruited families, conducted medical inspections and instruction, paid fares and subsidies, and transported emigrants to Santos. The report portrays most migrants as poor farming families, principally from Kyushu and Inland Sea prefectures, who began as plantation laborers in São Paulo and sometimes accumulated enough capital to become independent farmers. It contrasts the active Brazilian movement with limited settlement in Manchuria and concludes that the migration was socially significant but wholly inadequate as a solution to Japanese overpopulation.

subfiles.title: Japanese Settlement on the Lower Sungari
subfiles.doc_type: document file note and forwarding despatch
subfiles.from: G. C. Hanson, American Consul General, Harbin
subfiles.about: Forwards a despatch to the American Legation at Peiping concerning Japanese settlement on the Lower Sungari.
subfiles.summary: Hanson encloses a copy of his despatch no. 2750, addressed the same day to the Legation at Peiping. The forwarded study concerns Japanese settlement along the Lower Sungari in Manchuria, but its substantive text falls beyond this section.
